original.target_description: Study 1, Research Question 2: simple regression predicting positive well-being from social media use, US university students. Positive well-being is an average of satisfaction with life and positive affect; this is not life satisfaction alone. Predictor called social media use in the target paragraph without specifying SMEI versus SMT.

n.sample_role: University student participants; exact analytic n for target regression cannot be established
n.exclusions: Questionnaires with less than 50% completed or failed response checks were not retained (PDF p. 12). Usable N=304 conflicts with target regression degrees of freedom F(1,422); no analytic n inferred.
n.location: PDF pp. 14–16 (printed pp. 38–40), Demographics, Table 2 and Research Question 2
n.quote: The total sample of usable questionnaires consisted of N = 304 subjects. / Note: N = 304 for all measures

es.metric: beta (as printed; standardization not explicitly identified)

replication.target_description: Located p. 29 test: total screen time coefficient predicting life satisfaction in moderation model with extraversion and screen time × extraversion interaction, university students. Total screen time includes work, video viewing, gaming and smartphone use, rather than social media use specifically.

n.sample_role: University student participants; authors’ stated sample size for moderation model; internally inconsistent with printed residual df
n.exclusions: Missing values automatically removed from analyses (p. 35); around 50 participants excluded in most analyses (p. 36). Authors explicitly call 94 the moderation sample size, but also print F(3,94) and t(3,94); retained as stated and not verified by recalculation.
n.location: p. 35, Strengths and limitations, moderation-analysis sample discussion
n.quote: However, no significant effects were observed for the interaction term with a sample size of 94.

es.location: p. 29, Moderation analysis, total screen time main effect

p.location: p. 29, Moderation analysis, total screen time main effect

reported_success.location: pp. 29–30, Discussion, independent effects of screen time and comparison with Bunz (2021)
reported_success.quote: Counter to expectation neither total screen time nor active or passive social media use independently predicted life satisfaction. / These effects are generally not in line with the current literature (Bunz, 2021;

notes: Replication target_match=false: cited p. 29 coefficient belongs to total screen time in a moderation model, not specifically social media use. Authors’ negative narrative verdict concerns screen time/social media prediction of life satisfaction and explicitly compares with literature including Bunz. Original positive well-being combines life satisfaction and positive affect (PDF p. 13); retained as supplied broader positive well-being target. Original usable N=304 conflicts with F(1,422), so original analytic n is null. Replication n=94 is explicitly author-stated for the moderation model but conflicts with its printed residual df; confident=false. No sample sizes or effect sizes computed. Original beta preserved as printed without assuming standardization.
